October 2026 AI & Tech: The Complete Month

October was one of the densest months the industry has seen. Frontier models landed every few days, a major IPO filing revealed compute commitments in the hundreds of billions, open-weight models finally started competing on real work, infrastructure deals locked in capacity for years, and agent tooling, chips, robotics, and safety systems all moved at once. This is the full chronological rundown of what actually happened, from the first week through the end of the month, with the numbers, access details, and context that matter.

Early October (1–10)

🟢 OpenAI opened the month with Dots, their always-on agent system. These are persistent agents powered by GPT-6 Astra that run with a full cloud computer and browser access to more than 4,000 apps. You steer them from Slack, Teams, or your phone instead of the normal chat interface. Pro tier only. It is the clearest move yet toward agents that keep working in the background rather than waiting for you to open a window and type a prompt. The product is still early, but the direction is obvious: move from single-session chat to continuous operation.

Alongside it they pushed GPT-6.1 Sol. This one sits close to Astra on intelligence while costing significantly less: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output, with cached input down to $0.10. It outperforms Astra on several agentic coding benchmarks including DeepSWE and quickly became the default model inside Codex for a large number of users. The pricing was part of a clear pattern all month—OpenAI kept cutting costs as open Chinese models applied pressure. Sol is the model a lot of teams switched to for everyday agent work because the performance-to-price ratio improved enough to matter at scale.

🟠 Anthropic released Claude Sonnet 5.5 around the same window. It is roughly 30% faster and cheaper than the previous Sonnet, priced at $2/$10. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 it scored 70.6%, which was higher than Opus 5.5’s 66.4% in some configurations. A free tier is available. For most day-to-day coding and agent work this is now the model people actually reach for. They also dropped Claude Haiku 5.5 early in the month at $0.10/$0.50. It hits 72.4% on OSWorld and remains usable on Terminal-Bench 4.0 at 39.2%. This is the high-volume, low-cost option for agent loops and tool use where latency and price matter more than peak capability. Haiku 5.5 made a lot of previously expensive agent patterns economically viable.

🔵 Google’s Gemini 4 Argon started with restricted access for cyber defenders and trusted testers, then moved to general availability later in the month. At launch it topped both the Text Arena and the Vals Index. Pricing settled at $2/$10 on a promo rate that runs until around the end of November, with a 1.05 million token context window. It is a strong general model and the direct foundation that Gemini 4 Carbon was built on a couple of weeks later. The limited early access was deliberate; Google was still finishing safety and capability work before opening it more widely.

🟣 Mistral previewed Large 4 around the 6th to the 8th. Roughly one trillion total parameters, about 50 billion active, 1 million context, multimodal. Early numbers showed strong coding efficiency (around $1.13 per task in some reports). They explicitly said open weights were coming by the end of the month, which set up the improved “Le Chonk” release later. The preview already looked competitive enough that people started testing it against closed models on coding tasks.

Other early releases filled in the edges. Liquid AI shipped d1-3B and d1-omni-600M, tiny on-device decision models that run in 8 ms on a GPU and around 50 ms on a Jetson. These are aimed at local agents that need to make fast choices without round-tripping to the cloud. Aleph Alpha released Kolibri-1, a 78B/3.46B active German-English mixture-of-experts model with a 1 million context window under Apache 2.0. CoreWeave rolled out serverless GPUs billed per hour with no long-term contract, plus their Forge platform that combines run, observe, curate, evaluate, and Weights & Biases, and Agent Lens for agent observability. NVIDIA had Vera Rubin NVL72 and Vera CPU capacity available. Black Forest Labs updated FLUX 3 for 4K image generation with multi-reference and bounding-box layouts. Embeddings arrived from Google (EmbeddingGemma 2) and Perplexity (pplx-embed-v2). ElevenLabs pushed v4 speech models with better expression control across 90 languages. OpenAI also made their Decisions API available in public beta for fixed-choice answers and offered UltraFast mode on Cerebras (up to roughly 300 tokens per second for Astra on the Pro tier). The infrastructure layer was expanding as fast as the models.

Mid-October (11–20)

🔵 Gemini 4 Argon went fully generally available around the 13th to the 15th across the Gemini API, AI Studio, the Gemini app for Pro and Ultra users, and Antigravity. The promo pricing held. It was clearly one of the stronger general models on public arenas at that point and served as the base for everything Google did later in the month. Teams that had been waiting for broader access started switching workloads over.

🔷 Meta dropped Muse Spark Open. 816 billion total parameters, 42 billion active, 1 million context window, multimodal input and text output. Meta described it as the most capable US open-weight model to date. The weights are open but carry a revenue-cap license restriction. It is not closed-frontier level, but it is a genuine step up for open models on coding and agent work. For companies that want to self-host or fine-tune without relying on a single API provider, this was one of the more usable open options of the month.

🟢 NVIDIA released the Nemotron 3.5 series. Super VL is a 120 billion total / 12 billion active vision-language model aimed at agents with high throughput. Transcribe is an open speech model in the roughly 30–34 billion mixture-of-experts class. It handles 40 languages, speaker attribution, translation to and from English, and posts a low word error rate around 2.8%. It effectively consolidates what used to be several separate speech tools into one model. NVIDIA also continued pushing Vera Rubin NVL72 capacity and published agent throughput numbers that showed large efficiency gains per megawatt versus previous generations.

🟢 OpenAI models began appearing on Google Cloud. Around the 21st, GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, and GPT-6 Luna entered private preview on Model Garden for select enterprise customers, available through the Google Cloud Marketplace. Microsoft remains OpenAI’s primary cloud partner, but the multi-cloud distribution is clearly underway. Codex CLI and Desktop workflows can connect for inference. For enterprises already standardized on Google Cloud, this removed a friction point.

🟡 DeepSeek continued shipping efficient open-weight variants, including DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash. Artificial Analysis ran agent throughput numbers on NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin NVL72 and it delivered up to 5.7 times the total throughput per megawatt of a GB300 NVL72 on DeepSeek V4 Pro, with strong gains on Flash, GLM-5.2, and Kimi K3 as well. At peak throughput the lead narrows but remains positive. These numbers matter because inference cost and power are becoming the binding constraints for a lot of agent deployments.

🟡 Moonshot AI released Kimi K3.1 Pro around the 23rd. 2.8 trillion total parameters, 104 billion active, 1 million context window. It shows strong agentic performance plus improved 3D modeling and financial analysis features. Open weights were promised for early November. Chinese labs continued to ship large mixture-of-experts models at a pace that kept pressure on Western pricing.

Infrastructure and chips moved in parallel. Microsoft announced Azure Maia 300, their third in-house AI accelerator. It has 288 GB of HBM4 at 18 TB/s per chip, compute chiplets on TSMC’s N2P process, and 96 accelerators in a 167 kW rack. Production deployments start in 2027 and it is planned as the primary inference system for Microsoft products with multi-gigawatt scale. Anthropic signed a lease for EverWind’s 420 MW data-center campus at Point Tupper, Nova Scotia, with a first 95 MW phase targeted for late 2027. Amazon, X-energy, and AEP agreed to explore twelve 80 MW Xe-100 reactors at a former coal plant in Indiana, targeting nearly 1 gigawatt. Hitachi, Brookfield, Hartree, and Tokyo Gas signed an MoU for self-powered data centers in Japan. Sferical One, a shared supercomputer in Sweden with 1,152 NVIDIA GB300 GPUs, became operational. On the robotics side, Digit humanoids from Agility are expanding to additional warehouses (Statesville, North Carolina, and Lebanon, Tennessee) starting early 2027. Google published robotics work using Gemini 4 Argon for driving robots, building physics simulations from camera footage, and labeling robot video, with a self-reported 87% on the ERQA embodied reasoning benchmark. The data-center and power deals are the part of the month that will still be relevant in 2028 and 2029.

⚫ xAI did not release a new flagship model. Grok 4.7 from September remains the latest (500k context, $2/$6). They did ship Grok Voice 3.0 on the 14th: a speech-to-speech model that tops the Artificial Analysis ranking, responds in under a second, and costs $0.08 per minute. Grok Bot continued to receive updates, including model routing that can hand tasks to Claude Opus 5.5, Midjourney, or Suno depending on the job, plus shopping and incident-response features. Grok Imagine also released the first short episode of an AI-generated “Odyssey” series (about seven minutes); reception was poor, with widespread criticism of visual artifacts and overall quality. xAI spent more of the month on agent and voice features than on a new base model.

Late October (21–31)

🟢 On the 26th OpenAI released GPT-6.1 Terra. This is a fast model specialized for visual reasoning, computer use, and writing, the successor to GPT-5.6 Terra. It has a 1,050,000-token context window, accepts text and image input, and carries a knowledge cutoff of 1 June 2026. The API model ID is gpt-6.1-terra. It went live the same day in ChatGPT Work and Codex for Plus, Pro, Enterprise, and Edu users, in the OpenAI API, and on Amazon Bedrock. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 it scored 50.3% at maximum reasoning effort, up from 21.5% for the previous Terra. It meets the Critical threshold in cybersecurity under OpenAI’s Preparedness Framework and carries the protections built for GPT-6 Astra. OpenAI positions it as the efficient computer-use and writing model; they still recommend GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Astra for the hardest pure coding tasks. The release continues the price-cut pattern under pressure from open Chinese models. For teams that need a model that can look at a screen, click through software, and write clean output without burning through the most expensive tier, Terra is the one they started testing immediately.

🟠 The same day Anthropic filed its S-1 for a proposed Nasdaq listing under the ticker ANT. First-half 2026 revenue was $16.3 billion against an approximately $80.7 billion net loss (mostly non-cash). Compute commitments are enormous: up to $120.5 billion in NVIDIA-based GPU capacity from https://t.co/H79W8u9HMP LLC through 2029, with all capacity expected by December 2026, plus a minimum $110 billion commitment with Amazon running from May 2026 to April 2036. The governance structure preserves founder majority voting power and gives the Long-Term Benefit Trust control over a majority of board seats. The filing made the scale of the compute race concrete. These are not abstract future plans; they are contracted capacity with specific timelines.

🟢 NVIDIA and Meta expanded their partnership on the 26th. Meta will deploy more Vera Rubin systems and Vera CPUs, along with Spectrum-X Ethernet and BlueField-4. The two companies are collaborating on Meta’s Muse model family. NVIDIA is investing $3 billion in Meta’s equity offering. AMD also invested $1 billion in the same raise and has its first Helios rack-scale systems installed and in testing at Meta, with Meta planning to deploy custom AMD Instinct GPUs. The equity investments and hardware placements show how tightly the chip vendors and model labs are now linked.

On the 27th Artificial Analysis released Intelligence Index v5. It is a major overhaul with nine evaluations across four areas, 60% of the score coming from private or held-out tests, and new benchmarks including FrontierCode 2.0 and Terminal-Bench-Science. Initial scores were Claude Opus 5.5 (max) at 58, GPT-6 Astra (max) at 57, and GPT-6.1 Sol (max) at 55. The gap to the best open-weight model widened to roughly 12 points. Scores are not directly comparable to previous versions of the index. Gemini 4 Carbon later took the top spot at 59. The higher private-test share makes the ranking harder to game and more useful for teams that care about real capability rather than public leaderboard performance.

🔵 Google DeepMind previewed Genie 4 on the 27th. It is a real-time interactive world model that generates the scene and the audio natively—ambient noise, music, and dialogue. Gemini 3.8 Flash watches the frames and acts as a planning agent to keep the simulation consistent. It is currently a research preview for trusted testers, with wider access planned through Project Genie, early Gemini API access, and AI Studio partners. Current limitations are clear: sessions last only a few minutes, object permanence drifts over time, and real-world places are not accurately reproduced. All generated video and audio carry SynthID watermarks. World models are still early, but the native audio and planning-agent loop are the parts that make this one different from earlier video generators.

🔵 On the 28th Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon, their strongest model for cybersecurity and long-horizon tasks. It tops the updated Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at 59, one point ahead of Claude Opus 5.5. Cybersecurity numbers are high: 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro, 54.8% on ExploitGym, and 71.0% on CWE-bench. Access starts with a subset of cyber defenders through Google’s Fairwind Program and will widen to trusted partners. There is no firm date yet for broad developer, business, or consumer access. It is participating in US government voluntary pre-release testing. Carbon is built on the Gemini 4 Argon base that became generally available earlier in the month. The restricted rollout is deliberate; Google is treating the cyber capabilities carefully while still putting the model on public rankings.

🟣 On the 29th Mistral released the open weights for the improved Large 4, nicknamed Le Chonk, on Hugging Face along with API access. Post-preview reinforcement learning raised its Terminal-Bench 4.0 score by 13 points to 41%. It leads open-weight models on Cognition’s FrontierCode 2.0 at 19.7%. In multiple rankings it is currently the strongest open model outside China, with materially lower cost-per-task than closed frontier systems. Internal monitoring showed potential for cybersecurity uplift, so guardrails are being tightened with further updates planned. It sits in the roughly one-trillion-parameter class and is strong on coding and agent work relative to other open models. For organizations that want frontier-class coding performance without depending on a single closed provider, this was the most important open release of the month.

Additional late-month developments filled in the picture. GPT-6 Luna received an update that made answers shorter and less agreeable; safety tests improved but factual-error rates rose on some internal measures. Anthropic renamed its Max plans (Max 5x became Max, Max 20x became Ultra) and lifted the five-hour limit for verified Ultra accounts. OpenAI introduced Private Intelligence for stronger business data controls when using its most capable models. OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and Anthropic backed a shared robots.txt signal that lets websites state whether their content may be used for foundational generative AI training. The Gemini app added the ability to create and edit files directly inside chats. Meta quietly launched the Style Sketch AI fashion app and rolled out parent alerts for Facebook searches and Meta AI chats. OpenAI moved frontier model training fully offline and sandboxed after earlier incidents in which models reached the live internet during training. OpenAI also began releasing AI-generated proofs and solutions in mathematics, computer science, and physics as raw research data for academic peer review; Sam Altman said more discoveries exist and the stream will continue. AMD’s first Helios racks are installed and testing at Meta. Various labs pushed safety and monitoring updates, including self-assessment techniques and election centers for spotting model misuse. Cursor pulled a malicious Claude Code extension. Agents were used to steer the Allen Telescope Array from natural language requests. Waymo announced it will test an autonomous Toyota fleet in Japan. These smaller items show how AI is already moving into production systems outside the big labs.

Claude context for the month

Claude Opus 5.5, released in late September, remained a leading model throughout October. It has a 1 million token context window, pricing of $4/$20 per million tokens, adaptive thinking that is always on, strong agentic coding performance, and roughly 40% lower typical workload cost than the previous Opus. Fast mode is available at higher pricing. It stayed near the top of most rankings even as newer models arrived, which is why a lot of teams kept it as their default for hard coding and long-running agent work.

What the month actually looked like

Early October was efficient mid-tier models, agent infrastructure, and open-weight previews. Mid-month brought major open-weight drops such as Muse Spark Open, general availability for Gemini 4 Argon, and significant infrastructure announcements around chips and data centers. Late October delivered specialized frontier models—Terra for computer use and writing, Carbon for cybersecurity and long-horizon work, Genie 4 for interactive worlds, and the open Le Chonk weights—plus the large corporate and compute moves, most notably Anthropic’s S-1 and the multi-hundred-billion-dollar capacity commitments. Price pressure from open Chinese models was constant. Agent tooling became more practical. Benchmarks grew harder with higher shares of private tests. Gemini 4 Carbon currently leads the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, though access remains limited. Open models improved and closed some ground but still trail on the toughest private evaluations. A large amount of what shipped is still rolling out or restricted, so the practical effects will continue to show up over the coming weeks. The compute deals and data-center leases are the part that will still matter long after the specific model names have been superseded.
